subject: Seeking Advice on Reducing Data Size for openCR Analysis of Marine Mammals in the Open Sea

messages.author: 6b4487b0f22a71e5
messages.subject: Seeking Advice on Reducing Data Size for openCR Analysis of Marine Mammals in the Open Sea
parts:
Dear Murray,

I am currently encountering an issue while using the openCR::openCR.fit function in R, which results in the following error: 

Error in table(df$newID, df$newocc, df$newtrap, useNA = "no") : 
  attempt to make a table with >= 2^31 elements.

I believe the root of this error lies in the size of my effort table, which is approximately 8,000 × 1,000 (detectors by occasions). This large size is due to our survey track data not conforming to a spatially discrete structure, as observations are made continuously in space. Consequently, we have converted our survey track information into a grid-like array of detectors (Christiansen et al. 2015). The study area was divided into 1-km² grid cells, with each grid cell acting as a spatially distinct sampling unit (detector), similar to the approach described by Thompson et al. (2012).

Given this context, I am seeking advice on the following:

1. Is the error primarily due to the excessive number of detectors or occasions?
2. Would aggregating the surveys on a per week or per month basis be an appropriate solution to reduce the data size, and if so, what would be the best practices for doing this in the context of openCR?
3. Are there any alternative strategies or adjustments within openCR that could help manage such large datasets effectively?

This study focuses on the monitoring of marine mammals in the open sea, and any guidance on managing this data within openCR would be greatly appreciated.

All the best,

Rui Peres dos Santos

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Seeking Advice on Reducing Data Size for openCR Analysis of Marine Mammals in the Open Sea
parts:
Hi Rui Peres
Yes, that data structure is way too large for openCR (even if it didn't hit the R table limit it would take forever to fit), and yes, aggregating occasions would be a start. Perhaps also use coarser spatial discretization (2-km x 2-km?), assuming your animals move over several km. The reduce.capthist function should help with aggregating occasions.

We need better strategies for large open datasets. I started playing around with a moving-window approach (see ?moving.fit) but you're rather on your own there.
Murray
